notes:
I've written the notes below, verse by verse. Some limits up front: I couldn't get NET Bible notes, an Orthodox source (oca.org), or anything from Lutheran or Wesleyan-holiness sites. Coverage of vv. 9 and 13–16 is thin, and I found no source on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter. Where I name a commentator's tradition, the sources don't say so; that comes from me.

---

**Background to chapters 10–13**
- **Traditional view (Guzik):** Some think chapters 10–13 were once a separate letter. Guzik thinks this is unlikely but agrees the tone changes sharply. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **Reformed (TGC, Peter Balla):** Paul may simply have come back to the false apostles after dealing with the collection. Or fresh news about them may have reached him while he was writing, which would explain the change after chapter 9. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-corinthians/
- **Who the opponents were (Lowery, quoted on Precept Austin):** Any answer is tentative. They seem to have been Jews, but nobody knows where they came from. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-10-commentary
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):** Paul defends himself against "superapostles" who were promoting a gospel of triumph and success over his message of the cross. https://bibleodyssey.org/glossary/corinthians-the-second-letter-of-paul-to-the

---

**v. 1**
- **Matthew Henry:** Even under great provocation, Paul is humble and mild because of the meekness and gentleness of Christ. When we're tempted to be harsh, we should remember that same meekness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm
- **Guzik:** The critics compared Paul to a dog that barks loudly, but only from a distance. Boldness and lowliness aren't a contradiction; anyone who thinks so doesn't know the life of Jesus well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **Chrysostom (a Church Father honoured by both Catholics and Orthodox):** Paul is probably being ironic and repeating his critics' own words. His appeal to Christ's gentleness is meant to shame them. It shows that he holds back out of meekness, not because he lacks power. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** "Some" means not all the Corinthians thought badly of Paul; it may have been a loud minority. He also warns that people today who call themselves "apostles" cheapen the idea of apostolic authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **Chrysostom:** A teacher should be slow to punish and should aim at reform. Paul was hesitant even when he was defending the gospel, not himself. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm

**v. 3**
- **Chrysostom:** Paul doesn't say "we do not *live* by the flesh." He says "we do not *war* by the flesh": he is in a fight, but not with human weapons or human help. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Ministers live in the body like everyone else, but in their work they must not follow the flesh's rules. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm

**v. 4**
- **What the "weapons of the flesh" are:**
  - Chrysostom lists wealth, glory, power, fluency, cleverness, flattery and hypocrisy. Paul calls the weapons mighty "before God" because God made them so, not Paul. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm
  - Guzik says they aren't literal swords but the manipulative, deceptive methods his opponents used. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **The military picture (Ellicott):** The phrase is a military one taken from the Greek Old Testament. Paul may have been thinking of the idolatry of Corinth, or of the pride of individual opponents; Ellicott says the context favours the second. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/10-4.htm
- **Where Protestant teachers differ: what the weapons are**
  - Benson (a Methodist): mainly the word of God and prayer, made effective by the Holy Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/10-4.htm
  - Gill (a Baptist): the Scriptures, a whole armoury for both attack and defence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/10-4.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary: the "fortresses" were the resistance of hostile factions, which Paul hoped to overcome with apostolic authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/10-4.htm
  - Another commentator on the same page widens the list to church discipline, the sacraments and the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. The excerpt doesn't name this writer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/10-4.htm
- **Where Protestant teachers differ: what the strongholds are**
  - Gill: sin and Satan — unbelief, pride and hardness of heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/10-4.htm
  - Adam Clarke (a Methodist): the philosophers' persuasive reasoning. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/2-corinthians/10-4.html
  - Constable: probably the false arguments of Paul's opponents. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/10-4.html
- **Charismatic teachers disagree with each other:**
  - Chuck Smith (founder of Calvary Chapel) says we can pull down the enemy's strongholds through prayer, and that the battlefield is the mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/10-4.html
  - Sam Storms says some have wrongly read this text as being about territorial demons assigned to regions, which Christians must identify and pull down. He finds no basis for that here. He does think the passage connects to our conflict with spiritual powers who blind people to the gospel. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/taking-every-thought-captive-for-christ--2-cor--10:4-6-

**v. 5**
- **Chrysostom:** These strongholds besiege souls, not bodies; Paul means Greek pride and clever arguments. "Captivity" sounds harsh, but it leads from slavery to freedom. The aim is to win opponents over to the truth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm
- **Guzik:** In context Paul is talking about worldly thinking among Christians. The wider principle is that we aren't helpless victims of our thoughts; we can stop them and make them obey Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **Storms, quoting D. A. Carson:** The weapons destroy the mental patterns by which people live in rebellion against God. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/taking-every-thought-captive-for-christ--2-cor--10:4-6-
- **Adam Clarke's application:** Clarke saw the Reformation as this kind of victory, a pulling down of the papal system (cited by Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/

**v. 6**
- **Matthew Henry:** This isn't personal revenge. It means punishing disobedience to the gospel through church censure. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm
- **Chrysostom:** Paul waits until the faithful have separated themselves from the offenders, so that he doesn't punish them too. He even hopes the threat will reform the offenders. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm
- **Matthew Poole (quoted by Guzik):** This is a pattern for churches: don't rush to excommunicate, but go step by step. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** The Corinthians were using the wrong test. Testing an apostle is fine; judging only by appearances is not. Calvin adds that Paul was despised because he lacked the qualities the world admires. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **Matthew Henry:** However sure we are that we belong to Christ, we should allow that people who differ from us may belong to him too. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** Paul uses "boast" with a touch of sarcasm because talking about his own authority makes him uncomfortable. Christ gives authority in the church to build people up, not to tear them down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/
- **Matthew Henry:** Building up is the purpose of all authority, in church and state alike. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm

**v. 9**
- **Matthew Henry:** Paul is careful not to frighten them with big words or angry letters. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** The critics looked only at his appearance and listened only to his speaking style, not his message. He cites an early Christian description of Paul (perhaps around AD 200) as short, bald and bow-legged. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/

**v. 11**
- **Guzik:** If they won't change, they will get a consistent Paul, but a consistently severe one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/

**v. 12**
- **Calvin:** Paul is being ironic. The self-commenders lack true merit and claim to be what they are not. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_corinthians_volume_2/2_corinthians_10_12-18.htm
- **Guzik:** He applies this to pastors today: stop measuring yourselves against one another, whether that makes you feel superior or like a failure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/

**vv. 13–14**
- **Calvin:** The true measure of boasting is to stay within the limits the Lord has marked out. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_corinthians_volume_2/2_corinthians_10_12-18.htm
- **Reformation Study Bible (quoted on Precept Austin):** That measure includes Paul having come to Corinth as their apostle. It implies the opponents were intruding on his area of responsibility. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-10-commentary

**vv. 15–16**
- **Matthew Henry:** Paul hoped their faith would grow and the gospel would spread to regions beyond them, without his ever entering another man's field. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_010.cfm
- **Calvin:** Boasting in work "already done" means boasting in other people's labours: Paul fought the battle and they enjoyed the triumph. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_corinthians_volume_2/2_corinthians_10_12-18.htm
- **Guzik:** Paul stresses this probably because his opponents were doing exactly that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-10/

**v. 17**
- **Calvin:** Here "boasting in the Lord" means something different from 1 Corinthians 1:31. There it means crediting God for every blessing. Here it means leaving our glory entirely to God's judgment and counting everything else worthless. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_corinthians_volume_2/2_corinthians_10_12-18.htm
- **Storms:** By all means boast, but boast in the Lord. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/boasting--comparing--and-commending:-a-warning--2-cor--10:9-12-

**v. 18**
- **Calvin:** God alone has the right to judge us; we aren't fit judges of our own case. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_corinthians_volume_2/2_corinthians_10_12-18.htm
- **Adam Clarke:** The one not approved is the person who parades his own achievements and preaches himself rather than Christ. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv2-corinthians/10-18.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** They link the verse to Proverbs 27:2 and Jeremiah 9:23–24. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/10-18.htm
